# Aside: The Tucson Format {- .aside-chapter}

:::{.callout-note title="Draft"}
First draft, 2026-10-21. The broken file is made by `R/make-broken-tucson.R` and written to `data/co021broken.rwl`. Two things need dev dplR 1.8.1: the reader's warning about a missing stop marker (`NO_STOP_MARKER`) and the scale check at the end (`RWL_SERIES_SCALE`). Open questions are in the backlog.
:::

[Reading and Writing](03ReadingWriting.qmd) showed what the reader decided about two files. This aside is about what it was deciding between. The Tucson format is old, plain text, and forgiving to write by hand, which is why files in it go wrong. Once you know how a line is laid out, most of what can go wrong is visible in a text editor.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplR)
```
:::


## One Line at a Time

Here are the first lines of the Hurricane Ridge file, with a ruler on top so you can count columns.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
waLines <- readLines("data/wa082.rwl")
ruler <- paste0(rep(c(1:9, 0), 8), collapse = "")
tens <- paste0(sprintf("%10d", 1:8), collapse = "")
cat(tens, ruler, waLines[1:5], waLines[13], sep = "\n")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
         1         2         3         4         5         6         7         8
12345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890
712    1 Hurricane Ridge WIDTH_RING ABAM -
712    2 United States of America   Pacific silver fir 1560  4757-12328 1698 1983 -
712    3 FRITZ SCHWEINGRUBER -
712011  1811   153   138   142   152   142   135   150   107   128
712011  1820    90   109   154    99    87   127    94    65    75    78
712011  1900  -999    39    24    24    45    35    40    65    63    38
```


:::
:::


The first three lines are the header, which comes up below. After that every line is one decade of one series:

- Columns 1 to 8 are the series ID. Here it is six characters, 712011, and the next two columns are blank.
- Columns 9 to 12 are a year, the first year on the line.
- After that come up to ten measurements, six characters each, ending at column 72.

A decade line normally starts on a year ending in zero and holds ten values. The first line of a series starts wherever the series does, so 712011 begins in 1811 with nine values to fill out the decade. The last line ends with a stop marker. Nothing ties the lines of a series together except the ID repeated at the start of each one.

The numbers are whole numbers in units of the precision, so 153 is 1.53 mm. Where is the precision written? Only in the stop marker. A series that ends with 999 is in hundredths of a millimeter. A series that ends with -9999 is in thousandths. That one number at the end of the last line decides the scale of every value above it.

There are two more special values. A zero is an absent ring, a year in which the tree laid down no wood along that radius. A -999 inside a series is a year with no measurement, which is what 712011 has in 1900, the line at the bottom of the output. They look alike in a hurry and they mean very different things, and [Reading and Writing](03ReadingWriting.qmd) is about what happens when one is read as the other.

## The Header

The ITRDB puts three header lines at the top of a file. Each starts with the site code and a line number (712, then 1, 2 or 3), and the rest holds the site name, the variable and species code, the country and species, the elevation, the coordinates, the span, and the person who collected the wood. At Hurricane Ridge, `4757-12328` is 47°57' N, 123°28' W, written as degrees and minutes run together.

Nothing in the format marks a header as a header. The reader recognizes one because it doesn't parse as a decade line, and it keeps the three lines in the read record. Plenty of files have no header at all. Mesa Verde is one of them.

Where does the layout come from? Grissino-Mayer [-@GrissinoMayer2001] calls it the ring measurement, or "Tucson" or "Decadal", format, one of the ITRDB's standard formats, and says that COFECHA and the other DPL programs read it at either precision. Measuring programs write it, so most raw data you are given will be in it.

## A File With Known Defects

To see how files go wrong, I broke one on purpose. `R/make-broken-tucson.R` takes seven series from Mesa Verde for 1900 to 1963, writes them as a Tucson file, and then damages all but one series in a different way, each a mistake I have seen in files people sent me. Because I know what I did, we can check what the reader does with each one.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
source("R/make-broken-tucson.R")
planted <- make.broken.tucson()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
35 series, 1176-1963, 0.01 mm.
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
planted
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  series                                                             defect
1 641114                                                     none (control)
2 641121                 0.001 mm series with its -9999 stop marker missing
3 641132 nine-character ID (MV641132X) pushing the year out of columns 9-12
4 641143                                                1930s line repeated
5 642121          labeled 642114, sharing an ID and years with another core
6 642143                                          letter O for zero in 1920
```


:::
:::


The file is `data/co021broken.rwl`. Open it in a text editor alongside this aside, and see how many of the defects you can find by eye before the reader finds them.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
broken <- read.tucson("data/co021broken.rwl")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning: In data/co021broken.rwl, 5 line(s) hold a digit in column 72 and
another in column 73. Either the last measurement runs past the column-72
boundary, in which case truncating there drops a digit, or the record ends at
column 72 and what follows is not a measurement. The line does not say which,
and the reader takes the shorter reading: everything past column 72 is dropped.
Worth checking against the neighbouring years, since a value that is out of
range for its series is the sign that the digit belonged to it. First one:
MV641132X1900 15 35 0 25 1 26 21 34 27 3 <<past column 72>> 9
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning: In data/co021broken.rwl, 1 line(s) are exact copies of a line earlier in the file and were removed:
  641143  1930    21    20    21    11     5    25    14    21    17    15
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning: In data/co021broken.rwl, 7 line(s) were discarded because the year field does not read as a number and the line could not be read any other way. A line that reaches this point has already passed the header and length filters, so check whether it is a stray header or a data line whose columns are shifted:
  MV641132X1900    15    35     0    25     1    26    21    34    27    3
  MV641132X1910    43    35    52    27    48    54    52    49    20    4
  MV641132X1920    58    52    45    26    35    23    43    31    43    3
  MV641132X1930    35    25    36    14     8    24    17    27    27    2
  MV641132X1940    25    43    31    24    29    28    16    37    37    5
  MV641132X1950    19     9    34    13    22    24    22    32    29
  MV641132X1960    31    26    17    19   999
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning: In data/co021broken.rwl, 1 repeated series ID(s) had overlapping years and were renamed so that no measurements are lost:
  642114  decades 1900-1969  ->  642114X
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning: In data/co021broken.rwl, series 641121 ends without a stop marker (999
or -9999) on its last line. The stop marker is the only place the file states a
series' precision, so the reader assumed 0.01 mm. If it was measured to 0.001
mm, every value is ten times too large. rwl.check() compares the scale of each
series with the rest (RWL_SERIES_SCALE).
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning: In data/co021broken.rwl, core 642143, decade starting 1920: 1
measurement(s) are not numeric and are left as NA.
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Interior gaps: 1 year(s) with no measurement, in 1 of 6 series.
  642143  1 year in 1 gap: 1920 (1)  file holds no value in the file
  Returned as NA. The file records no measurement for these years,
  which is not the same as a ring width of zero.
  Pass fill.internal.NA = 0 to fill them with zero, as read.tucson.legacy() does.
  See help for details.
6 series, 1900-1963, 0.01 mm.
```


:::
:::


That's a lot of output for a 50-line file. The reader is noisy on purpose. Every one of those warnings is also kept in the read record, so you don't have to catch them as they scroll past.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
brokenRecord <- attr(broken, "dplR.provenance")
brokenRecord$events[, c("event", "series", "n")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
           event series n
1     PAST_COL72   <NA> 5
2 DUPLICATE_LINE   <NA> 1
3       BAD_YEAR   <NA> 7
4     ID_RENAMED   <NA> 1
5 NO_STOP_MARKER 641121 1
6    NON_NUMERIC 642143 1
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
brokenRecord$renames
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
     old     new               why
1 642114 642114X overlapping years
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
names(broken)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "641114"  "641121"  "641143"  "642114"  "642114X" "642143" 
```


:::
:::


How did the reader do against the table of what I planted?

- The repeated 1930s line in 641143 is an exact copy of the line above it. The reader removed it and said so (`DUPLICATE_LINE`). A copy that differed in even one value would be a different problem, two values for the same year, and the reader would report that as a clash.
- Two cores labeled 642114 cover the same years. The reader can't know which is which, so it kept both and renamed the second one 642114X (`ID_RENAMED`), and the renames table says so. Which core was really 642121 is something only the field notes can tell you.
- The letter O typed for a zero in 642143 isn't a number. The reader left that year as `NA` and said where (`NON_NUMERIC`), which makes it a gap in the middle of the series.
- The nine-character ID cost the most. MV641132X runs into column 9, so the year field holds "X190" and the last digit of the last value on each full line lands in column 73. The reader couldn't make sense of the lines and discarded all seven of them (`BAD_YEAR`, `PAST_COL72`), so 641132 isn't in the result at all. It is not quietly misread, though. The warning prints every line it dropped.

So the reader caught four of the five defects. The fifth is 641121, the series that lost its -9999, and it is the hard one. The reader noticed that the series ends without a stop marker and said so (`NO_STOP_MARKER`), but noticing is all it can do. The marker was the only place the file said the series was in thousandths, so with it gone the reader fell back on hundredths, and the warning tells you that's what it assumed. Up to `dplR` 1.8.0 it made the same assumption and said nothing.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
brokenRecord$precision
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   series precision
1  641114      0.01
2  641121      0.01
3  641143      0.01
4  642114      0.01
5 642114X      0.01
6  642143      0.01
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
round(colMeans(broken, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 641114  641121  641143  642114 642114X  642143 
   0.26    3.00    0.25    0.20    0.23    0.23 
```


:::
:::


Every series is recorded at 0.01 mm, and 641121's mean ring is 3.00 mm against about 0.24 for the others. Ten times too wide. And the crossdating statistics won't save you here, because a series ten times too large has exactly the same correlation with the others as the series itself. Of the defects in the file, this is the one the reader can't fix, because the file no longer holds the answer.

So which is it, a series in the wrong units or a fast-growing tree? The scale says. `rwl.check` compares each series' median ring with the median of the others, and warns when one is five times off or more.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
brokenCheck <- as.data.frame(rwl.check(broken))
brokenCheck[brokenCheck$check == "RWL_SERIES_SCALE", c("series", "value")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  series    value
8 641121 12.08333
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
cat(strwrap(brokenCheck$message[brokenCheck$check == "RWL_SERIES_SCALE"]), sep = "\n")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
median ring width 2.9 mm is 12.1 times the median of the other series
(0.24 mm). A factor near 10 is what a lost -9999 stop marker or a
series in the wrong precision produces; a fast or suppressed tree
rarely differs this much. Check the units of this series before using
it
```


:::
:::


Why five, when the error is ten? Because a lost stop marker multiplies whatever the series was, and a slow tree that was half the width of its neighbors comes back only five times wider. Trees that grow five times faster or slower than the rest of their stand are rare, though not unheard of, so a series flagged at five is a series to look at, and one near ten deserves a hard look at its units. When I ran the check over the ITRDB's ring-width files, a few hundred series in about 2 percent of files were five times off or more, and a handful of files had series ten times off. Before 1.8.1, nothing in `dplR` flagged any of them.

In this file there is a second clue in the editor, since every value of 641121 ends in a zero. That's because I made it from data measured to the hundredth, and a series measured to the thousandth won't give you that clue.

## When a File Reads Strangely

Open it in a text editor before you blame the reader. Count columns. Look at the end of each series for its stop marker, and at the start of each line for an ID that's too long or a year that's in the wrong place. Most of what goes wrong in a Tucson file is a column out of place, and you can see that faster than any program can describe it.
